title: Double Binds: The Tensions Between Black Activism, Collective Responsibility, and Individual Choice
author: Ceci Bell
summary: Ceci Bell reads Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay as an example of a double bind, a no-win situation created by contradictory demands, in which Black parents must choose among educational quality, racial belonging, individual opportunity, and collective responsibility. She argues that the answer to why families still face this choice is policy, and that Hannah-Jones's attempt appears to have been a solo project without enough community buy-in. Drawing on Gloria Ladson-Billings's idea of an education debt, Linda Darling-Hammond's work on unequal resources, and David Labaree's three purposes of schooling, she frames the dilemma as a question of how educational resources are distributed. She cites a Michigan Senate candidate on property-tax funding and redlining, and H. Richard Milner's distinction between schooling and education. Bell closes by connecting the case to the double binds facing Black scholars committed to community engagement.
points: Bell locates Hannah-Jones's dilemma in systemic policy failures that no single family can solve.
Ladson-Billings's education debt reframes achievement gaps as the accumulated result of historical and political decisions.
Labaree's tension between education as a public good and as private advantage sits at the center of the choice Hannah-Jones faced.
Property-tax school funding tied to redlined property values is offered as a concrete mechanism of inequity.
Bell asks whether community support for children risks becoming an excuse for public systems not to meet their obligations.
quotes: For me, the deeper question is why Black families are still asked to choose between educational quality, racial belonging, individual opportunity, and collective responsibility. The answer is spelled P-O-L-I-C-Y.
The ideals that led Hannah-Jones and her husband to make the educational choices they made for their child were rooted in inequities that one family cannot solve.

Resource allocation sits at the center of educational equity. Without adequate, equitable distribution of resources, many of the other reforms we debate become difficult, if not impossible, to realize.

Hannah-Jones’s dilemma sits squarely within that tension. What happens when our commitment to education as a collective public good conflicts with our responsibility to secure the best opportunities we can for our own children?
What happens when we ask individual Black families to compensate for educational debts and resource inequalities that individual families did not create and cannot solve?

Hannah-Jones’s story is not simply about which school Najya attended. It is also about what educational opportunities, knowledge, support, and preparation were actually available to her once she got there.

The policy question is not whether communities should stop supporting children. Black communities have a long history of educating, mentoring, tutoring, organizing, and building institutions. The question is whether community support becomes an excuse for public systems not to meet their own obligations.
